div.p: Earliest Deadline First (EDF) is an optimal scheduling algorithm for uniprocessor real-time systems. Improved Quick Processor-demand Analysis (QPA*) provides efficient and exact schedulability tests for EDF-scheduled systems with arbitrary relative deadlines. The values of the dividing points can significantly affect the performance of QPA*. In this paper, we provide an efficient approach based on experiments to find suitable values of the dividing points; we also investigate the best value of the dividing points by extensive simulations on a large number of randomly generated task sets. We show that the proposed approach can significantly reduce the required calculations to perform a dividing point's value selection.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: The most important attribute of real-time systems is that the correctness of such systems depends on not only the running results but also on the time at which results are produced. Real-time systems have to guarantee that all the strict timing requirements must be satisfied. In other words, real-time systems have timing requirements that must be guaranteed. Scheduling and schedulability analysis enables these guarantees to be provided.

The most common dynamic scheduling scheme for realtime systems is Earliest Deadline First (EDF) which was introduced by Liu and Layland [4] in 1973. According to the EDF algorithm, an arrived job with the earliest absolute deadline is executed first. The EDF algorithm has been proven [2] to be optimal among all scheduling algorithms on a uniprocessor, in the sense that if a real-time task set cannot be scheduled by EDF, then this task set cannot be scheduled by any algorithm.

Quick Processor-demand Analysis (QPA) [8] provides fast and exact schedulability tests for general EDF systems. By extensive experiments [8], we showed that QPA decreases the required calculations exponentially compared with previous results on exact schedulability tests; the required calculation load for QPA is stable for all kinds of task sets.

Improved Quick Processor-demand Analysis (QPA*) [9] which is based on QPA. QPA* can significantly reduce the required calculations to perform an exact test for unschedulable systems, and the computation required by QPA* for schedulable systems is nearly the same as QPA. Hence the required calculations for general EDF systems can be significantly decreased by QPA*.

The motivation for providing faster exact schedulability analysis for general EDF systems is two-fold. As part of the design process many different parameter profiles may need to be checked. An automated search may even be undertaken as part of the architectural definition of the system. An efficient but accurate schedulability scheme is therefore needed. The second requirement comes from online systems. During the run-time of a system there could be new tasks arrive that need (if possible) to be added to the task set. The system must recalculate schedulability online to decide whether to allow the new tasks to enter into the system. The decisions have to be made in a short time and should not occupy too much system resource.

QPA* divides the checking interval into two or more sub-intervals, the schedulability of system is tested by finding failure time points in each time interval. Hence, the value of dividing points can significant affect the performance of QPA*. However, finding the best value of dividing points require extensive simulations and it needs the QPA* test to be executed a large number of times at every possible value, hence, the process is expensive and is not applicable to practice.

In this paper, we provide an efficient approach based on experiments to find suitable values of the dividing points. We show that the proposed approach can significantly reduce the required calculations to perform a dividing point's value selection.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 describes the system model and notations used in this paper. Section 3 describes the existing results on exact schedulability analysis for EDF systems with arbitrary relative deadlines. Section 4 presents our approach of the dividing points selection, and we use the proposed approach to investigate the suitable values based on a large number of task sets. Conclusions are provided in Section 5.

At any time, an arrived job with a higher priority can preempt a lower priority job's execution. When a job completes its execution, the system chooses the pending job with the highest priority to execute. According to the EDF algorithm, the released job with the earliest absolute deadline is assigned the highest priority.

div.head: D. Conclusion from the Investigations
div.p: This section provides an efficient approach based on experiments to investigate the suitable values of dividing points for different types of task sets. From the experimental results of this section, we can see that the task parameters can obviously affect the best value of x L for QPA*. Since the best value of x L is changed according to variable conditions, in order to get the best performance of QPA*, we may need to select the values of dividing points according to the task sets' properties.

According to the experimental investigations of this section, if we do not perform the dividing points selection for the task sets, 0.1L , 0.36L , and 0.46L are suitable values of x L for most arbitrary task sets, most ( 80% > ) unschedulable task sets can find failure in these time intervals.

div.head: V. CONCLUSIONS
div.p: QPA* provides efficient and exact schedulability tests for EDF-scheduled real-time systems. The values of dividing points can significant affect the required computations by QPA*. However, the dividing points value selection needs to perform a large number of schedulability tests at every time point in the interval (0, ) L to decide which value is most suitable for QPA*. This is expensive and sys-tem designers need an efficient approach to choose suitable values of dividing points for QPA*.

In this paper, we provide an efficient approach based on experiments to find suitable values of dividing points; we also investigate the best value of dividing points by extensive simulations on a large number of randomly generated task sets. We show that the proposed approach can significantly reduce the required computations to perform a dividing point's value selection.
